extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and researchers interested in number theory
extracted.subtask_description: Describes the definition, properties, conjectures, theorems, empirical data, and major results about twin primes (pairs of primes that differ by 2). Intended as an encyclopedic summary of known facts, conjectures, and recent progress in the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of twin prime
rubrics_metrics.description: A twin prime is a prime number that is either 2 less or 2 more than another prime number (i.e., a prime with prime gap of two). Sometimes the term is used for a pair of twin primes (a prime twin or prime pair). Examples: (17,19), (41,43).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: The pair (2,3) is usually not considered a twin prime pair because 2 is the only even prime; twin primes are the closest-spaced primes other than that exceptional pair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form-of-large twin primes: 6n±1 representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Every twin prime pair greater than (3,5) is of the form (6n−1, 6n+1) for some natural number n; the number between the two primes is a multiple of 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence: the sum of any twin prime pair (other than (3,5)) is divisible by 12. The constraint also implies digit-ending and modular restrictions on n (discussed below). Example first pairs: (3,5),(5,7),(11,13),(17,19),… (OEIS: A077800).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brun's theorem (convergence of reciprocals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Viggo Brun (1915) showed the sum of reciprocals of the twin primes is convergent (Brun's theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significance: First application of the Brun sieve and foundational for modern sieve theory. Quantitative consequence: one can obtain an upper bound on the number of twin primes less than N of order CN/(log N)^2 for some constant C>0. A refined upper bound is (8 C_2 N/(log N)^2)[1+O((log log N)/(log N))], where C_2 is the twin prime constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twin prime conjecture (infinitely many twin primes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The twin prime conjecture states there are infinitely many primes p such that p+2 is also prime (equivalently, infinitely many twin prime pairs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a long-standing unsolved problem. de Polignac (1849) gave a more general conjecture that for every k there are infinitely many primes p with p+2k prime; the k=1 case is the twin prime conjecture. Stronger distributional forms (Hardy–Littlewood) predict an asymptotic law for twin primes. Partial progress: Zhang (2013) proved existence of infinitely many prime pairs with bounded gap ≤ some N (initially 70 million), and subsequent work (Maynard, Tao, Polymath) reduced the bound; current unconditional liminf of prime gaps ≤ 246. Under Elliott–Halberstam-type assumptions the bound can be reduced further (to 12 or 6 as stated by Polymath wiki under different hypotheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: First Hardy–Littlewood conjecture and twin prime constant
rubrics_metrics.description: A special case of the first Hardy–Littlewood conjecture predicts π_2(x), the number of primes p≤x with p+2 prime, satisfies π_2(x) ~ 2 C_2 x/(ln x)^2 as x→∞, where C_2 is the twin prime constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twin prime constant: C_2 = ∏_{p prime, p≥3} (1 - 1/(p-1)^2) ≈ 0.6601618158468696…. The conjecture is justified heuristically by modeling prime density as 1/ln t (from the prime number theorem). The fully general prime k-tuple conjecture implies this asymptotic; the second Hardy–Littlewood conjecture is mentioned to be false in full generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zhang/Maynard/Tao bounded gaps results and improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Yitang Zhang (2013) proved there exists an integer N < 70,000,000 such that infinitely many pairs of primes differ by at most N; Maynard and Tao produced simpler approaches and bounds for related functions f(m) guaranteeing infinitely many intervals of width f(m) containing ≥m primes. Polymath and subsequent work reduced the unconditional bound to 246.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These results are major improvements on earlier analytic methods and give unconditional bounded-gap results (not yet down to 2). Under additional hypotheses (Elliott–Halberstam or generalized forms) the bounds can be reduced further (to 12 or 6 in Polymath discussions). Zhang's work was accepted rapidly and spawned collaborative improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goldston–Pintz–Yıldırım (GPY) and small-gap results
rubrics_metrics.description: Goldston, Pintz, and Yıldırım (and earlier partial results by Erdős) proved there are infinitely many pairs of consecutive primes with gaps smaller than c ln p for some constants c<1, and later improvements made c arbitrarily small in a particular normalized sense: lim inf_{n→∞} (p_{n+1}-p_n)/ln p_n = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: Infinitely many prime gaps are much smaller than average (average gap ~ ln p). However, these results do not imply infinitely many gaps equal to 2; they instead show the existence of arbitrarily small normalized gaps. Under hypotheses like Elliott–Halberstam they can show more structured small-gap patterns (e.g., infinitely many n with at least two primes among certain small admissible k-tuples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Polignac's conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Polignac's conjecture (1849) states that for every positive even integer k, there are infinitely many consecutive prime pairs with difference k (i.e., infinitely many prime gaps of size k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The twin prime conjecture is the k=2 case. Zhang's result shows Polignac's conjecture is true for at least one even k (some unknown value), because bounded-gap results forbid arbitrarily large gaps eventually.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical data and large twin primes (computational records)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distributed computing projects (Twin Prime Search, PrimeGrid) have located record-large twin primes; as of the page's update, the largest known twin prime pair is 2996863034895×2^1290000 ± 1 (388,342 decimal digits). There are counts (e.g., 808,675,888,577,436 twin prime pairs below 10^18) and empirical analyses of the function f(x) in counts of pairs showing trends toward the conjectured constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical analyses suggest f(x) (in π_2(x) = f(x)·x/(ln x)^2) decreases from ≈1.7 for small x toward ≈1.3 as x→∞, conjectured to approach 2C_2 (≈1.3203236…). Large-record searches use distributed computation and produce press releases and archives (PrimeGrid, Prime Pages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary properties, congruences, and modular/digital constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Various elementary facts: every third odd number divisible by 3 so no three consecutive odd numbers can all be prime (hence 5 is the only prime part of two twin pairs). The lower member of a twin pair is a Chen prime. A pair (m,m+2) is a twin prime iff 4((m−1)!+1) ≡ −m (mod m(m+2)). For twin pairs of form (6n−1,6n+1) with n>1, n must end in digits 0,2,3,5,7,8 (not 1,4,6,9) in base 10 to avoid divisibility patterns; similar modular restrictions hold modulo any prime p≥5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules give quick divisibility and digital-pattern checks that rule out many candidates; they are elementary number-theoretic constraints useful in sieving and heuristic reasoning about distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated primes and density consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: An isolated prime (non-twin) is a prime p such that neither p−2 nor p+2 is prime (examples: 2,23,37,…).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brun's theorem implies 'almost all' primes are isolated in the sense that the ratio of isolated primes below n to all primes below n tends to 1 as n→∞ (i.e., twin primes have zero natural density among primes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations to prime k‑tuples, triplets, and Chen primes
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and relationships: if m−4 or m+6 is prime as well, three primes form a prime triplet. The lower member of a twin prime pair is a Chen prime (a prime p such that p+2 is prime or product of at most two primes under Chen's theorem contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article mentions prime k-tuples and twin primes as instances; many conjectures and conditional results apply to admissible prime k-tuples, and results on small gaps often address occurrences of multiple primes within small admissible patterns.
